IN THE
Supreme Court of the United States

Nos. 25-238, 25-566
CUTBERTO VIRAMONTES, ET AL., Petitioners,
v.
COOK COUNTY, ILLINOIS, ET AL., Respondents.
________________________
EDDIE GRANT, JR., ET AL., Petitioners,
v.
RONNELL HIGGINS, ET AL., Respondents.
____________
On Writs of Certiorari
to the United States Court of Appeals
for the Second and Seventh Circuits
________________________
BRIEF OF THE CITY OF CHICAGO AND 23
OTHER CITIES AND COUNTIES AS AMICI
CURIAE IN SUPPORT OF RESPONDENTS
____________
INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici represent American cities  and counties
working to fight the devastating effects of mass
shootings and to keep the most lethal firearms off
their streets:  Austin, Texas; Baltimore , Maryland;
Boston, Massachusetts; Boulder, Colorado; Boulder
County, Colorado; Chicago, Illinois; Cincinnati, Ohio;
Columbus, Ohio; Evanston, Illinois; Los Angeles,

1 No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in part,
and no person other than amici made a monetary contribution to
its preparation or submission.

2


California; Madison, Wisconsin; Martin Luther King
Jr. County, Washington; Minneapolis, Minnesota;
New Haven, Connecticut; Pima County, Arizona;
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania;  Portland, Oregon; San
Diego, California; San Diego County, California; San
Francisco, California; San Francisco County,
California; Santa Clara County, California; Seattle,
Washington; Tucson, Arizona.
Amici have suffered extensive loss of life, threats
to public safety  and law enforcement, disruption to
their economies, and substantial health care costs
from mass shootings and other firearms violence.
Assault rifles, such as AR -15s, have proliferated on
city streets and have been used to inflict serious
injuries and death on a massive scale.
Communities of all sizes are vulnerable to mass
shootings. R esidents live side -by-side, share public
parks and plazas, stroll sidewalks, attend schools and
houses of worship together, and gather on “Main
Streets” for parades and other community events.
Densely populated cities are particularly vulnerable.
With popu lations in the hundreds of thousands or
millions, they are home to numerous public gathering
places and host festivals, rallies, and other large
events that draw millions of tourists each year. Public
events like these have become targets of mass
shootings.
Many amici have adopted ordinances banning
assault rifles or are located in states that have
enacted bans, and gun owners and advocates are
increasingly challenging these bans in state and

3


federal courts across the country. One such lawsuit
currently pending seeks to invalidate Chicago’s
ordinance. See Herrera v. Raoul , 1:23-cv-00532 (N.D.
Ill.). In that case, the Seventh Circuit upheld the
denial of a preliminary injunction on the ground that
the plaintiff was not likely to succeed on the merits of
his Second Amendment claim. See Bevis v. City of
Naperville, 85 F.4th 1175 (7th Cir. 2023). 2 That case
is stayed in the district court pending the outcome
here. Amici therefore have a strong interest in
ensuring that they can maintain effective regulations
in response to the dangers that extraordinarily lethal
weapons pose to the public peace and safety within
their borders.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The challenged laws must be upheld. From the
founding era th rough the present day, lawmakers
have enacted restrictions on weapons that are
dangerous and unusual, are disproportionately
misused in criminal activity, and disrupt the public
peace and order. Bans on assault rifles are justified by
the same regulatory pr inciples. Assault rifles are
extraordinarily dangerous devices that have been
used by perpetrators of mass shootings to inflict
unimaginable carnage in public places. Not only have
they taken the lives of numerous Americans, but they
have instilled terror, disrupted the public peace, and

2 In Viramontes v. Cook County, No. 24-1437, 2025 WL 1553896
(7th Cir. June 2, 2025), the plaintiffs argued that Bevis should be
overruled. Id. at *3. The court held that the plaintiffs failed to
offer any compelling reason to do so. Id.

4


imposed significant costs on communities and local
governments. Assault rifles  also pose a grave threat
to law enforcement officers who are tasked with
securing public events and who must face these
weapons on city streets.
Any burdens the challenged laws may impose are
commensurate with those imposed by the historical
laws. They target a specific problem created by a
specific class of weapons: misuse of assault rifles in
deadly mass shootings and other violent crime. And
because assault rifles are extraordinarily lethal, bans
on these weapons in public and private spaces are
critical to protect against physical and psychological
harm and to ensure the public’s freedom to participate
in shared social and political life. The decisions below
should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
Our nation’s historical tradition reveals an
unbroken line of restrictions on dangerous and
unusual weapons used to disrupt the public peace and
safety, from early English common law through the
present day . Modern-day bans on assault rifles fit
comfortably within this tradition.
Historical Tradition Supports Restrictions on
Assault Rifles in Public and Private Spaces.
In New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass ’n v. Bruen ,
597 U.S. 1 (2022), the Court held that, to satisfy the
Second Amendment, “the government must
demonstrate that the regulation is consistent with

5


this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm
regulation.” Id. at 17. This analysis requires
“reasoning by analogy.” Id. at 28. “[A] historical
regulation is a proper analogue for a distinctly modern
firearm regulation” where the two “are relevantly
similar,” id. at 28-29 (quotation omitted), looking at
“how and why the regulations burden a law -abiding
citizen’s right to armed self-defense,” id. at 29. As this
Court has explained, analogical reasoning under the
Second Amendment is not “a regulatory straight -
jacket,” meaning the government need not identify “a
historical twin.” Id. at 30. Further, in “cases
implicating unprecedented societal concerns or
dramatic technological changes,” it is necessary to
take “a more nuanced approach.” Id. at 27.
In United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680 (2024),
this Court reinforced Bruen’s methodology, clarifying
that it was “not meant to suggest a law trapped in
amber.” Id. at 691. Rather than mandating
“regulations identical to ones that could be found in
1791,” Bruen merely asks “whether the challenged
regulation is consistent with the principles that
underpin our regulatory tradition.” Id. at 692; see also
id. at 739 (Barrett, J., concurring) (“To be consistent
with historical limits, a challenged regulation need
not be an updated model of a historical counterpart.”);
id. at 740 (Barrett, J., concurring) (“Historical
regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.”). This
analysis is not “mechanical,” Wolford v. Lopez , 609
U.S. 185, 197 (2026); “[i]t undeniably necessitates an
exercise of judgment,” id., a measure of “common
sense,” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 698, and “sensitivity” to
the challenges of applying the historical record  to

6


modern affairs, United States v. Hemani , 608 U.S.
772, 782 (2026).
When properly applying this Court’s precedents,
it is plain to see that restrictions on assault rifles
satisfy Bruen’s “why” and “how”; they are justified by
the same principles that underpin our nation’s
regulatory tradition, and any burdens the challenged
laws may  impose are commensurate with those
imposed by the historical laws.
A. Three Principles Underpin Our Nation’s
Tradition of Arms Regulation.
As this Court observed in Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 694,
the Anglo-American tradition of arms regulation
traces its roots to the Statute of Northampton, which
read, in part:

[N]o man great nor small . . . [shall] be so
hardy to come before the King’s Justices,
or other of the King’s Ministers d oing
their office, with force and arms, nor
bring no force in affray of the peace, nor
to go nor ride armed by night nor by day,
in fairs, markets, nor in the presence of
the justices or other ministers, nor in no
part elsewhere.
Mark A. Frassetto, To the Terror of the People: Public
Disorder Crimes and the Original Public
Understanding of the Second Amendment, 43 S. Ill. U.
L.J. 61, 62 (2018) (quoting Statute of Northampton, 2
Edw. 3 c. 3 (1328 (Eng.)).

7


Enacted in 1328, the Statute of Northampton
built upon existing common law restrictions on “going
or riding armed.” Patrick J. Charles, The Faces of the
Second Amendment Outside the Home: History Versus
Ahistorical Standards of Review , 60 Clev. St. L. Rev.
1, 11 (2012). The Statute was enforced in England at
least into the eighteenth century, id. at 23 -30;
Frassetto, supra, at 67, and was carried across the
Atlantic by the English colonists and incorporated
into colonial and early American jurisprudence,
Frassetto, supra, at 66; Darrell A.H. Miller et al.,
Technology, Tradition, and “The Terror of the People,”
99 Notre Dame L. Rev. 1373, 1383-84 (2024). For that
reason, “the founding -era understanding of the
Statute of Northampton is an extremely important
consideration for determining the original public
understanding of the right to keep and bear arms at
the time of the ratification of the Second Amendment.”
Frassetto, supra, at 63.
Three principles emerge from the historical record
of the Statute of Northampton and its adoption into
American law. First, “[t]he power to regulate and in
some cases prohibit dangerous or unusual weapons
has always been central to the police power
authority.” R. 81 -17 at 26 ( Viramontes). 3  Second,
lawmakers have responded to community concerns
about weapons with regulations, including bans, once

3  We cite the records from the decisions below as R. ___
(Viramontes) and R. ___ ( Grant). We cite the records in Barnett
v. Raoul , No. 3:23 -cv-00209 (S.D. Ill.),  Herrera, No. 1:23 -cv-
00532, and National Association for Gun Rights v. Lamont , No.
3:22-cv-01118 (D. Conn.), as R. ___  (Barnett), R. ___ ( Herrera),
and R. ___ (NAGR), respectively.

8


those weapons “circulate[d] sufficiently in society to
spill over into criminal or other harmful use.” R. 52 -
12 ¶ 33 ( Herrera). Third, throughout history, it has
been “the government’s prerogative to regulate
weapons . . . to preserve public peace and public
order.” Joseph Blocher & Reva B. Siegel, When Guns
Threaten the Public Sphere: A New Account of Public
Safety Regulation Under Heller, 116 Nw. U. L. Rev.
139, 143, 164 (2021).
1. Prohibitions on carrying dangerous
and unusual weapons.
Lawmakers and legal commentators throughout
the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries understood
the Statute of Northampton  as prohibiting the
carrying of dangerous or unusual weapons in terrorem
populi, or “to the terror of the people.” Miller et al.,
supra, at 1384. Queen Elizabeth I responded to the
proliferation of pistols, daggers, and other weapons
that were capable of causing the “‘good quiet people’”
to be “‘ in feare and danger of their lives,’” by calling
for strict enforcement of the Statute, and tied “the
need to enforce the law directly to ‘the terror of all
people professing to travel and live peaceably.’”
Frassetto, supra, at 67  (quoting By the Que nne
Elizabeth I: A Proclamation Against the Common Use
of Dagges, Handgunnes, Harquebuzes, Calliuers, and
Cotes of Defence  1 (London, Christopher Barker
1579)).
Two of the most influential  legal scholars of the
eighteenth century, William Blackstone and William
Hawkins, popularized this  reading. Blackstone, in

9


describing the Statute of Northampton, wrote that
“‘[t]he offence of riding or going armed, with
dangerous or unusual weapons, is a crime against the
public peace, by terrifying the good people of the
land.’” Miller et al., supra, at 1384 (quoting 4 William
Blackstone, Commentaries 148 (1769)). Hawkins used
similar terms. He wrote that the “crime of affray,”
referenced in the Statute, is “committed ‘where a Man
arms himself with dangerous and unusual Weapons,
in such a Manner as will naturally cause Terror to the
People.’” Frassetto, supra, at 69 ( quoting 1 William
Hawkins, A Treatise of the Pleas of the Crown  135
(1721)). See also Saul Cornell, The Right to Keep and
Carry Arms in Anglo -American Law: Preserving
Liberty and Keeping the Peace , 80 Law & Contemp.
Probs. 11, 19-20 (2017) [hereinafter, “Cornell, Right to
Keep and Carry Arms ”] (“[N]o man, great or small,
shall go or ride armed, by night or by day, with
dangerous or unusual weapons, terrifying the good
people of the land.”) (quotation omitted)).
Blackstone, Hawkins, and other scholars of their
day used the phrases “dangerous or unusual” and
“dangerous and unusual” interchangeably. R. 59 -7
¶ 20 (Grant) (emphases added). These two phrases are
“an example of the grammatical and rhetorical form
hendiadys.” Id. Hendiadys is a form of speech, popular
in the founding era, “that uses two independent words
connected by a conjunction . . . to express a single
concept.” Id. ¶ 20  n.45. Readers would have
interpreted “dangerous or unusual” and “dangerous
and unusual” to mean the same thing – “a ban on
weapons that were ‘unusually dangerous.’” Id. ¶ 20.
Indeed, the sorts of firearms and daggers that Queen

10


Elizabeth I prohibited would have been unusually
dangerous at that time, as they were especially lethal
compared to other weapons and increasingly used in
criminal activity. R. 37-6 ¶¶ 27, 30 (NAGR).
These are also the sorts of weapons that would
have caused terror, even without any corresponding
act of violence. Any weapon has the potential to be
dangerous, but “the Statute of Northampton was not
regulating dangerous conduct.” Charles, supra, at 20.
It was prohibiting “the act of arming in the public
concourse” in a way “that terrified the people.” Id. As
Blackstone noted, “‘terrifying the good people of the
land’ – not just attacking them – was itself ‘a crime.’”
Blocher & Siegel, supra, at 165 (quoting Blackstone,
supra, at 149). Hawkins, too, confirmed that “‘there
may be an Affray where there is no actual Violence; as
where a Man arms him [s]elf with dangerous and
unusual Weapons. ’” Charles, supra, at  23 (quoting
Hawkins, supra, at 135 ). Blackstone and Hawkins
were not alone; other respected scholars of the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries shared their
view of the Statute and its terror element. Frassetto,
supra, at 76-82.
Thus, the view that carrying unusually dangerous
weapons was a threat to the public order that could be
criminalized was well entrenched in England
precisely at the time the colonists were creating their
own bodies of law in the New World. The colonists
“drew liberally ” from “English texts,” including
“popular English legal guides.” Saul Cornell, The
Persistence of Common Law Limits on Armed Travel
in the Early Republic : Surety and Affray Laws in

11


Historical Context, 78 SMU L. Rev. 343, 352 (2025)
[hereinafter, “Cornell, Common Law Limits”]. Indeed,
the earliest weapons restrictions were based on the
Statute of Northampton, id.; Frassetto, supra, at 71;
Miller et al., supra, at 1384, and in some cases “copied
Northampton’s ‘to the terror’ prohibition,” Blocher &
Siegel, supra, at 167, or borrowed other language from
the Statute “almost verbatim,” Charles, supra, at 32;
see also Cornell, Right to Keep and Carry Arms, supra,
at 32 (early laws “followed closely on [their] English
predecessor”).
For example, in 1686, New Jersey  “prohibit[ed]
‘rid[ing] or go[ing] armed with sword, pistol or dagger’
because those going armed put ‘several persons . . . in
great fear.’” Frassetto, supra, at 71 (quoting An Act
Against Wearing Swords, etc., ch. 9, 1686 N.J. Laws
289, 289-90); see also Miller et al., supra, at 13 89-90
(“New Jersey prohibited the carrying of ‘any Pocket
Pistol, Skeines, Stilladers, Daggers or Dirks, or other
unusual or unlawful Weapons,’” in response “to public
outcry against the practice of a few who were putting
the rest of the colony ‘in great Fear .’” (same)).
Massachusetts and New Hampshire  soon followed
suit, calling for the arrest of anyone who shall “‘go
armed offensively.’” Frassetto, supra, at 71 (quoting
An Act for the Punishing of Criminal Offenders, no. 6,
1694 Mass. Laws 12); Miller et al., supra, at 1390
(quoting An Act for the Punishing of Criminal
Offenders (1701), reprinted in Acts and Laws, Passed
by the General Court or Assembly of his Majesties
Province of New -Hampshire in New -England 14, 15

12


(Boston, Eleazar Ruffell 1716)). 4  And after the
Constitution was ratified , Virginia, Massachusetts,
Tennessee, Maine, and North Carolina all enacted
laws based on the Statute of Northampton. Miller et
al., supra 1384 (citing An Act Forbidding and
Punishing Affrays, ch. 49, 1786 Va. Acts 35; Act of
Jan. 29, 1795 ch. 2, 1795 Mass. Acts 436; Act of Nov.
13, 1801, ch. 22, § 6, 1801 Tenn. Acts 259, 260-61; Act
of Mar. 15, 1821, ch. 76, § 1, 1821 Me. Laws 285, 285);
Charles, supra, at 31 -32 (citing Francois Xavier
Martin, A Collection of Statutes of the Parliament of
England in Force in the State of North -Carolina, 60-
61 (Newbern 1792)).
Like their English predecessor, these colonial and
early American laws targeted the carrying of
especially lethal weapons, suitable for criminal
activity, as those were the weapons that would have
struck fear. Scholars confirmed that “a substantial
motivating factor” for modelling laws on the Statute
of Northampton was “the fear created by the carrying
of firearms in public,” Frassetto, supra, at 71, and
that, under these laws, “overt acts,” “violence or
threats of violence,” or “injury” to persons or property
were not necessary, as the carrying of dangerous and
unusual weapons “alone was terrifying,” id. at 82.
Popular legal guides, including justice of the peace
manuals, echoed these concepts. For example, they
borrowed the English law of affray, which “did not

4 Going “armed offensively” meant carrying firearms and edged
weapons “in contrast to shields and armor, ” which were
“defensive weapons. ” Cornell, Common Law  Limits, supra, at
351.

13


require actual violence,” but was committed simply by
carrying “dangerous and unusual armaments” in
public “in such a way to cause terror of the people.”
Miller et al., supra, at 1386-87.5
2. Restrictions on weapons that are
misused in criminal activity.
In the founding era, “[i]nterpersonal violence,
including gun violence, simply was not a problem . . .
that warranted much attention.” Saul Cornell, The
Right to Carry Firearms Outside of the Home:
Separating Historical Myths From Historical
Realities, 39 Fordham Urb. L.J. 1695, 1713 (2012)
[hereinafter, “Cornell, Right to Carry Firearms ”].
Homicide rates in general were “low among colonists”
just before the American Revolution, R.  37-6 ¶ 14
(NAGR), and the proportion of “homicides committed
with firearms was correspondingly low – between 0
and 10 percent,” id. ¶ 20; see also id. ¶ 17 (“Guns were
not the weapons of choice in homicides that grew out
of the tensions of daily life.”). Colonists rarely carried
loaded firearms, “except to hunt, control vermin, or
serve in the militia,” id. ¶ 20, and the muzzle-loading
muskets and fowling pieces owned by most colonists
“had significant limit ations as murder weapons,”
since they were slow to load, could not fire multiple
shots without reloading, were not accurate at long
ranges, and were prone to misfiring, id. ¶ 16. In short,

5  Justice of the peace manuals “proliferated” during the
founding and “provide some of the best accounts of popular
understanding of Anglo -American principles in this period.”
Cornell, Right to Keep and Carry Arms, supra, at 13.

14


“there was not a serious homicide problem looming
over debates about the Second Amendment.” R. 81-17
at 10 (Viramontes).
While homicide rates briefly spiked during the
American Revolution, once the war was over,
“homicide rates fell to levels in some instances even
lower than those which had prevailed in the early and
mid-eighteenth century.” R. 37 -6 ¶ 20 ( NAGR). But
“[t]he early decades of the nineteenth century
witnessed a revolution in the production and
marketing of guns.” R. 81 -17 at 11 (Viramontes). The
same “market revolution” that made an “astonishing
assortment of manufactured goods readily available
. . . also transformed gun culture,” Cornell,  Common
Law Limits, supra, at 350, as “cheap, reliable, and
more lethal firearms” became “widely available for the
first time in American history,” id. at 348.
These new firearms, like percussion -cap pistols
and revolvers, were concealable  and easier to load,
could be kept loaded for long periods of time, and were
overall deadlier. R. 37 -6 ¶¶ 25, 30 -33 ( NAGR). And
Americans “began sporting” them “with alarming
regularity.” R.  81-17 at 11 ( Viramontes). Deadlier

“Bowie-related mythology” and the knife’s “distinctive

integral part of the American way of life,’” Barnett v.
Raoul, 180 F.4th 1035, 1047 (7th Cir. 2026) (quoting
Harold L. Peterson, American Knives: The First

15


Unsurprisingly, during the late 1840s and 1850s,
homicide rates “exploded across the United States.” R.
37-6 ¶ 28 (NAGR). Public officials realized these new

of the era’s murders and serious assaults.” Id. ¶ 24.
Lawmakers across the country responded with “a

(Viramontes), as well as restrictions on Bowie knives
and other long -bladed weapons, R. 52 -12 ¶¶ 70 -71
(Herrera); see generally R. 247 -1 ( Barnett). Some

weapons, id., while others enacted more sweeping
restrictions, like Massachusetts, which “effectively
prohibited the right to travel armed,” unless “an
individual had a reasonable fear of imminent
violence,” a model that “was emulated by ” Delaware,
Maine, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Oregon, Minnesota,
and the District of Columbia, Cornell, Right to Carry
Firearms, supra, at 1720. And some lawmakers
banned certain weapons outright.  Georgia, for
instance, made it unlawful “‘to sell, or offer to sell, or
to keep, or to have ’” a number of weapons, including
pistols and Bowie knives. R.  247-1 at 31 ( Barnett)
(quoting 1837 Ga. Acts 90, An Act to Guard and
Protect the Citizens of this State, Against the
Unwarrantable and  too Prevalent use of Deadly
Weapons § 1); R. 37-6 ¶ 26 (NAGR) (same).
From the 1850s through World War I, “the
proportion of homicides committed with firearms
continued to climb, ” due in part to the advent of
modern breech-loading firearms. R. 37-6 ¶ 34 (NAGR).
Legislatures responded with “a staggering range of

16


new laws to regulate arms.” R. 81 -17 at 18
(Viramontes). In fact, the number of laws enacted
increased by “ [400%] from antebellum levels.” Id. at
18. By the start of the twentieth century, “virtually
every state in the country prohibited or severely
restricted concealed gun [s] and other weapons
carrying,” and “several states barred possession of
such weapons outright.” R. 52-12 ¶ 48 (Herrera).

the proliferation of the Thompson submachine gun.
Developed during World War I, submachine guns
represented a dramatic technological advancement
over existing multi-shot firearms, as they “were light
enough to be carried and operated by a single
individual” and capable of firing from large -capacity
magazines “at a rate of 600 to 725 rounds per minute.”
R. 37-6 ¶ 45 (NAGR). By the mid-to-late 1920s, when
“ownership spread in the civilian population,” R.  81-
17 at 21 ( Viramontes), criminals “quickly discovered
how accessible and useful these new technologies
were,” R. 37-6 ¶ 46 (NAGR). They became the weapons
of choice for gangs, bank robbers, rebels, and terrorist
groups, and were used most notoriously in the 1929
St. Valentine’s Day Massacre slaying in Chicago. Id.
“Federal, state, and local officials and law
enforcement officers suddenly confronted novel
threats to their personal safety,” R. 37-6 ¶ 46 (NAGR),

17


ownership of machine guns and submachine guns ,”

72-103 (Barnett).
3. Weapons regulations that protect
the public peace and order.
Restrictions on weapons “to preserve public peace
and public order” have “deep roots” in the Anglo -
American tradition, and “[t]his longstanding
sovereign prerogative shaped weapons laws long
before the Founding of our constitutional democracy
and the writing of the Second Amendment.” Blocher
& Siegel, supra, at 164. Indeed, the Statute of
Northampton, as well as the founding -era laws it
propagated, named public terror, not violence, a s the
central concern , and was understood to protect the
public peace and order, not merely physical safety. As
Blackstone observed, carrying dangerous and unusual
weapons to terrify the people was itself “‘a crime
against the public peace.’” Id. at 165 (quoting
Blackstone, supra, at 149).
The “fairs” and “markets” of concern in the
Statute of Northampton “were important sites of
community life” in fourteenth -century England.
Blocher & Siegel, supra, at 165. They were shared
spaces, located in populous places, where “‘a great
concourse of the people’” would gather. Cornell,
Common Law Limits, supra, at 352 (quoting Statute
of Northampton, 2 Edw. 3, c. 3 (1328) (Eng.)). Going
armed with the sorts of weapons apt to strike terror
in these places disrupted the “public order and

18


community life” and undermined “the liberty and
security of the polity.” Blocher & Siegel, supra, at 164.
Even after the adoption of the English Declaration of
Rights in 1688, “[t]he scope of the right to carry arms,”
even “for reasons of self -defense,” was “balanced
against the need to preserve” the peace. Cornell, Right
to Keep and Carry Arms, supra, at 13.
As is evident from the colonial and early American
laws prohibiting the carrying of weapons that strike
terror, the founders adopted the English approach to
weapons regulation that prioritized public peace and
order. Blocher & Siegel, supra, at 164. As the founders
enshrined the right to bear arms, the scope of that
right “was still shaped by the [English] common law
tradition, including the necessity of preserving the
peace.” Cornell, Right to Keep and Carry Arms, supra,
at 13. Simply put, any “liberty interest in the right to
arms was always balanced against the concept of
peace.” Id. at 14; see also Miller et al., supra, at 1395
(“[T]he tradition of American weapon regulation [has
been] geared toward s the preservation of the peace
and the maintenance of political and public life free
from fear.”). Even when an individual could
demonstrate a specific need to carry a weapon for selfdefense, he was required to post a “peace bond” to
ensure he would keep the peace. Saul Cornell, The
Long Arc of Arms Regulation in Public: From Sureties
to Permitting, 1328 -1928, U.C. Davis L. Rev. 2545,
2570-71 (2022).
The need to preserve the public peace and order
remained a central tenet of weapons regulation as
new and more terrifying weapons began to proliferate

19


in American society in the nineteenth century. States
began broadly prohibiting weapons in “places of public
congregation” and at “social gathering[s].” Miller et
al., supra, at 1393. The Oklahoma Territory, for
example, banned weapons where people assembled
for amusement, or for educational or
scientific purposes, or into any circus,
show or public exhibition of any kind, or
into any ball room, or to any social party
or social gathering, or to any election, or
to any place where intoxicating liquors
are sold, or to any political convention, or
to any other public assembly.
Id. at 1394-95 (quoting Okla. Stat. ch. 25 , art. 47, § 7
(1890)). Other states, like Missouri and Arizona,
passed similarly sweeping bans. Id. at 139 4 (citing
Mo. Rev. Stat. § 1274 (1879); Ariz. Rev. Stat., Penal
Code § 387 (1901)). And courts confirmed that public
carry restrictions like these were aimed not just at
preventing violence but preserving citizens’ freedom
to gather peacefully in public places. See, e.g., Aymette
v. State, 21 Tenn. (2 Hum.) 154, 159 (1840) (upholding
legislature’s authority to prohibit individuals armed
with “drawn swords, guns, and fixed bayonets” from
entering a theater or church and “break[ing] up” these
“public assemblages”).
B. Restrictions on Assault Rifles Are
Justified by the Same Regulatory
Principles.
The same principles that underpin the historical

20


tradition justify the challenged bans on assault rifles.
First, assault rifles are dangerous and unusual
weapons. They are extraordinarily lethal to the public
and pose exceptional risks to law enforcement.
Second, assault rifles are disproportionately misused
in criminal activity. They are the weapons of choice in
mass shootings and other violent crime that
devastates cities. Third, assault rifles are a significant
threat to the public peace and order. They cause terror
and disrupt our social and political fabric.
1. Assault rifles are extraordinarily
lethal and pose exceptional risks to
law enforcement.
Extraordinary Lethality . AR -15s and similar
assault rifles trace their roots directly to the Armalite
AR-15, which was developed for the U.S. Army in the
1950s and used in the Vietnam War. R. 81 -4 ¶ 96
(Viramontes). The Army invited Armalite to design “a
lightweight, high-velocity rifle, that could operate in
both semi - and full-automatic modes with firepower
capable of penetrating a steel helmet or standard body
armor at 500 yards.” Id. After “a comprehensive field
evaluation,” R. 52-6 ¶ 26 ( Herrera), the weapon was
lauded for its light weight, maneuverability, low
recoil, accuracy, high capacity, and ability to fire
bullets at an extremely high velocity , id. ¶¶ 30 -34
(Herrera); R. 52 -7 ¶ 32 ( Herrera). Its “lethality” and
“reliability record were particularly impressive,” and
the wounds it created “were prodigious.” R. 81-4 ¶ 97
(Viramontes). Designed for “maximum wound effect,”
id. ¶ 101, the bullets could “travel nearly three times
the speed of sound,” R.  52-6 ¶ 34 ( Herrera), creating

21


“catastrophic injuries” to the human body, id. ¶ 27.
The “phenomenal lethality” of the Armalite AR-15
led the Army to adopt it and rebrand it as the M16, R.
81-4 ¶ 99 ( Viramontes), with minimal modifications,
R. 185 -1 ¶ 40 ( Barnett), and the AR -15 used by
civilians today retains all of the “aspects that made it
such a valuable lethal weapon for deadly combat,”
R. 81-4 ¶ 100 (Viramontes). In fact, the only difference
is that the AR -15 lacks the fully automatic mode. Id.
But that is not a distinction that makes AR -15s any
less dangerous; on the contrary, semiautomatic fire
can be more lethal. According to the Army, the
preferred combat mode for an M16 is semiautomatic,
id., because it “allows targeting of specific human
targets with repeated accurate shots ,” R. 52 -7 ¶ 34
(Herrera), and thus “more accurately, effectively, and

For all these reasons, the AR -15 has been

¶ 101 ( Viramontes). When a bullet from an AR -15
strikes the body, “the payload of kinetic energy rips
open a cavity inside the flesh,” R. 52-6 ¶ 34 (Herrera),
“creating a large temporary cavity whose maximum
diameter is up to 11 -12.5 times the diameter of the
projectile,” R. 81-5 at 18 (Viramontes). Once inside the
body, “one assault weapon round can destroy organs

R. 52-10 ¶ 35 (Herrera). Bones can be “shattered” and

Even “[i]njuries to blood vessels, nerves, or organs not

occur.” R. 81-5 at 17 (Viramontes). Shots “to the head,

Mitch Smith, A Chicago Neighborhood Faces a New
Fear: Assault-Style Rifles, N.Y. Times, May 11, 2017 ,
https://www.nytimes.com/2017/05/11/us/guns-chicago
-violence-rifles.html. The spate of violence left “ the
police overwhelmed and residents ever more wary of
venturing outdoors.” Id. Remarked the local
alderman: “People are walking around traumatized
[with a] glazed look, like they’re not sure what to
expect, not certain of what’s going to come out from
behind the shadows at any given moment.” Id.

33


C. Any Burdens the Challenged Laws May
Impose Are Commensurate with Those
Imposed by the Historical Laws.
Any burdens imposed by bans on assault rifles are
commensurate with those imposed by the historical
laws, meaning they satisfy the “how” of Bruen’s
methodology. Like the weapons regulations of
previous generations, the challenged laws target a
specific problem created by a specific class of weapons.
Assault rifles are extraordinarily lethal, are
disproportionately misused in mass shootings and
other violent crime, and disrupt the public peace and
order. Bans on these weapons are critical not only to
protect the public from physical harm, but also to
protect the public’s freedom to enjoy and feel safe in
their communities and participate in shared so cial
and political life – liberties that our lawmakers and
leaders have cherished since the founding.
While many of the historical laws prohibited only
public carry, modern laws need not impose
restrictions that are “identical” to founding -era laws.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 69 2. Bruen allows for a more
flexible, commonsense approach that takes into
account “unprecedented societal concerns” and
“dramatic technological changes.” 597 U.S. at 27. Both
of these factors are present here. No weapon at the
founding could inflict the type of devastation  that
assault rifles can, R. 52-13 ¶¶ 8, 31, 60, 65 ( Herrera),
and as we explain, mass shootings themselves are a
modern phenomenon.
Moreover, the urban areas we know today did not

34


exist at the founding; cities did not densify until the
late 1800s, Joseph Blocher & Eric Ruben,
Originalism-By-Analogy and Second Amendment
Adjudication, 133 Yale L.J. 99, 154 (2023), and “there
were no police departments,” id. at 156. Many families
lived alone on isolated farms or on frontiers with
muskets and fowling pieces for hunting and killing
pests. R. 81-17 at 9 (Viramontes); see also Wolford, 609
U.S. at 192. Thus, while encountering unusually
dangerous weapons in public caused terror and
disrupted social life, there would have been little
concern about weapons kept indoors.
Assault rifles, however, can devastate the public
even from interior spaces. For one, their high-velocity
bullets can “easily penetrate[ ]” walls, R. 52 -9 ¶ 99
(Herrera), posing “a substantial risk to individuals in
adjoining rooms, neighboring apartments o r other
attached dwelling units,” id. ¶ 101, particularly in
dense urban areas, R. 61-1 at 64 (Herrera). Their long
range and extreme firepower also enable assailants to
fire multiple rounds at law enforcement officers, at
passersby, or into crowds, while concealed in upper -
story windows or on rooftops – like the Las Vegas
shooter who fired more than 1,000 rounds in minutes
from the 32nd floor of a hotel overlooking a music
festival, killing 58 and wounding 800. R. 81 -15 at 4
(Viramontes).
Indeed, many public spaces where Americans
gather are particularly vulnerable to mass shootings
from windows and rooftops.  In major cities, tall
buildings tower over parks and beaches that host
concerts, festivals, rallies, and other special events

35


and are crowded daily with locals and tourists.  At
major events, like Lollapalooza in Chicago, as many
as 400,000 attendees pack into Grant Park in the
shadow of Michigan Avenue’s high rises.  The
possibility that a perpetrator could be perched
undetectably on an upper floor of a high rise presents
a significant threat . And this threat is not unique to
major cities. Suburbs and small towns host parades,
festivals, and concerts along their main streets, where
a perpetrator could just as easily be hiding in an upper
story window or on the rooftop of a commercial
building, as occurred in Highland Park, Illinois,
where the perpetrator fired 83 rounds from an AR-15
in under 60 seconds onto paradegoers, killing seven
and wounding 48. R. 52-2 ¶ 19 (Herrera).
Furthermore, even when assault rifles are stored
in private homes, the risk of criminal misuse is high.
Many of the assault rifles wielded by perpetrators of
mass shootings or used in other criminal activity were
stolen from private homes. For example, of 20 school
shootings in which data is available, the perpetrators
in 17 of those incidents obtained their weapons from
the home of a relative, R. 81 -4 ¶ 51, including the
perpetrator of the Sandy Hook Elementary School
shooting, who stole assault rifles lawfully owned by
his mother and used th em to kill 2 7 children and
teachers, R. 52-4 ¶ 14 (Table 2) (Herrera); R. 81-4 ¶ 86
(Viramontes). In fact, “it is orders of magnitudes more
likely that a criminal will steal a gun of a law-abiding
citizen than a law -abiding citizen will fire an assault
weapon in lawful self -defense.” R. 81 -4 ¶ 108
(Viramontes).

36


None of these things concerned the founders
because none were a problem. Indeed, as Justice
Barrett put it, “‘[t]he regulatory challenges posed by
firearms today are not always the same as those that
preoccupied’ earlier generations.” Wolford, 609 U.S. at
220 (Barrett, J., concurring) (quoting Bruen, 597 U.S.
at 27).  Colonial lawmakers targeted “the particular
misconduct that they happened to confront,” but
today, firearms are “misused in other ways that were
unknown to our forebears but pose an equivalent risk
to persons or property,” id. (Barrett, J., concurring) –
or in the case of assault rifles, a far greater risk.
Bruen also allows for different solutions to
account for the fact that “societal perception of the
problem” may have changed. Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 705
(Sotomayor, J., concurring). The historical laws
already sought to quell fear, and now our
understanding of fear and the psychological trauma
that firearms violence can have on survivors,
witnesses, and community members has developed
further. We now have a greater understanding and
respect for depression, anxiety, PTSD, and other
mental health disorders. Wulf Rössler, The Stigma of
Mental Disorders: A Millenia -Long History of Social
Exclusion and Prejudices , EMBO Reports, Jul . 28,
2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5007
563/. And because the colonists and early Americans
were not connected through social media and
inundated with news stories about violent crime,
there was no  comparable opportunity for collective
trauma to ripple through communities miles away
from the criminal acts. Today, we understand that
assault rifle bans in both public and private places are

37


critical not just to ensure physical safety and quell
fear, but to ensure mental and psychological health.
Mass shootings cause collective trauma and profound
social damage. As long as the weapons that facilitate
these horrific incidents remain in circulation, the
possibility of a mass shooting will continue to loom
over our heads.
In short, founding -era lawmakers made certain
policy choices about how best to protect the public
from dangerous and unusual weapons, weapons
misused in criminal activity, and weapons that
threaten the public peace and order, based on the
circumstances of life in the eighteenth century, the
scope of the firearms problem, and lawmakers’
understanding of the threat to the public. Modern
lawmakers are entitled to make choices that account
for present -day needs , even if they lack a precise
historical analogue . As Justice Barrett observed,
Bruen does not demand that present -day regulations
“follow late-18th-century policy choices,” nor assume
that founding -era lawmakers “maximally exercised
their power to regulate.” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 739 -40
(Barrett, J., concurring). So long as modern
lawmakers respond to the threat of firearms with
“‘focused regulations’ to address the threat,” Wolford,
609 U.S. at 220 (Barrett, J., concurring) (quoting
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 700), the law passes muster.
The challenged laws are focused regulations that
address the physical and psychological devastation of
assault rifles. And because assault rifles are n ot
suitable for and are rarely used i n self-defense, and
because numerous other, more suitable weapons

38


remain available for that purpose,  R. 81-4 ¶¶ 19, 59 ,
115-18 (Viramontes), any burden the challenged laws
may impose is minimal. They must be upheld.
CONCLUSION

The judgments below should be affirmed.
